text: bo2-mac Call of Duty: Black Ops II, statically recompiled from 32-bit x86 Windows to native ARM64 macOS. Campaign, Zombies and multiplayer against bots, built on your Mac from your own Steam copy. English · 中文 Abstract · Method · Limits · Repository · Legal Beta, 2026-11-03 · measured on one Apple M1 (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores, 16 GB) Campaign (Angola), Zombies (Town) and multiplayer (Hijacked, against bots) on an Apple M1, recorded while playing; the number in the top right corner is frames per second, and the screen recording itself costs some, mostly in the campaign. 80-second video (MP4, 20 MB) Important This repository contains no game file and no translated game code. It turns your own Steam copy of Black Ops II into an app for your Mac, on your Mac. The game's code ends up inside that app, so nobody can hand you a ready-made one: each player builds their own, and it may not be shared. Unofficial fan project, not affiliated with Activision, Treyarch or Microsoft. To play, buy the game. Beta: read what has and has not been proven . bo2-mac takes the three executables of Black Ops II, the campaign ( t6sp.exe ), Zombies ( t6zm.exe ) and multiplayer ( t6mp.exe ), and turns their x86 machine code into ARM64 machine code ahead of time. Remill lifts each function to LLVM IR, a chain of our own passes rewrites that IR, and the result is linked with a Win32 runtime written by hand, whose Direct3D 11 is drawn by Metal. There is no Wine and no JIT: the game runs as native code, in one process. About 150,000 functions are translated across the three executables. Only the short sequences that the copy protection hides run in a small x86 interpreter, and so does any code the translation missed, so a hole is built to cost speed rather than crash the game. On an Apple M1 the campaign runs at 51–60 frames per second , and every mission loads and hands over to the next one, down to the end credits. Zombies is played solo on six maps through the game's own menus at 57–60 . Multiplayer is played against bots through its real menus, eleven game modes, at 53–60 . One app, Black Ops II.app , opens the campaign, and the CAMPAIGN / ZOMBIES / MULTIPLAYER entries of each menu switch to the other game. Nothing is downloaded from anyone but you: the converter reads the executables of the copy you bought, checks them byte for byte, and builds the app on your machine. Frame rate counts the drawables really presented to the screen, checked against the screen and the Metal HUD. What you can play All three modes: keyboard and mouse, or a DualSense as XInput through GameController.framework; sound on; movement keys follow their position on your keyboard (ZQSD on AZERTY, WASD on QWERTY), unless you bound them yourself in the game's options. In five steps, all on the player's Mac: The copy protection is executed, not bypassed. The game hides integrity checks behind hardware exceptions, single-step traps and code it decrypts into the heap. A small x86 machine built on Unicorn ( x86_guest_vm.cpp , heap_code.cpp ) runs exactly those sequences and hands control back to the recompiled code. No check result is forced and no key is placed by hand. A hole in the translation is built to cost speed, not a crash. When the game reaches x86 code that was never lifted, the same machine runs its original bytes ( interp.cpp ) and gives control back to the recompiled code at the next translated block, call or return. Each interpreted address is logged ( [INTERP] ). The online service is answered locally. Zombies and multiplayer expect Demonware; a responder written from the game's own requests ( dw_local.cpp ) answers the lobby, storage and ticket on your Mac. Nothing leaves the machine. They translate Windows calls at run time and keep the x86 code under Rosetta. Here the x86 code itself is gone: it is ARM64 machine code before the game starts. DXVK and DXMT are PE DLLs that reach their native backend through Wine's unixlib mechanism; this port has no Wine, and its Direct3D 11 is its own layer over 32-bit guest memory. Only shader translation was needed from outside, and HLSLcc, a plain C++ library, covers it. Each entry is a symptom seen on screen, the cause that was measured, and the effect of the fix. F1 · The lifter ignored the x87 rounding mode. In Zombies the prone view shook. fistp rounded to nearest where the game had asked for truncation, inside the network codec of the view height. The height received by the client was wrong on 8 samples out of 8, and on 0 out of 8 after a Remill patch and a re-lift of the codec. F2 · One reserved bit of the x87 control word. A campaign mission froze in an effects loop, only with real threads. The lifter stored bit 6 of the control word differently from real hardware. A one-line Remill patch and four re-lifted runtime functions fixed it, with no slowdown. F3 · A CPU feature flag changes the algorithm. Our IsProcessorFeaturePresent answered "no SSE2", so the C runtime took its x87 ceil , which rounded to nearest under our runtime. An effect then sampled index −1 forever: two missions froze. F4 · Our own log caused the stutter. Hitches of 170–430 ms were the render thread blocked in write() : our log, redirected to a file on a nearly full disk. Sending it through a pipe to a child process took the hitches per run from 12 and 8 to 0 and 0. F5 · Shader translation moved constants by 4 bytes. HLSLcc placed a float2 after a float at offset 24 where Direct3D reads it at 20. 31 of 2,664 shaders were affected, among them the eyes and the reticles. F6 · The protection has to run. The options menu froze 8 times out of 8. An integrity check rewrites its own return address to point at code decrypted into the heap, which the runtime ignored. Running that code, as Windows does, gave 3 out of 3 without a freeze. F7 · Our own safety guards were the obstacle. One guard of ours stopped the game at 28 seconds of play. The largest gains of the project came from removing our own guards and false sharing, not from clever code. F8 · An empty API stub looks like a broken service. Two stubs that returned nothing ( CryptGenRandom , StringFromGUID2 ) looked like a network failure in Zombies. F9 · Thread priorities are part of the program. SetThreadPriority was a stub. Passing the mixer's request to macOS cut the short audio buffers of a run from 908–1872 to 7–71, and the sound gaps with them. F10 · Native skinning, bit for bit. CPU skinning rewritten in NEON gives the same bits as the original x86 and took a heavy scene from 17.8 to 30.3 fps. F11 · Decals need the game's depth bias. Scorch marks and blood appeared or vanished with a slight turn of the camera. The game asks for a depth bias on decals; our layer left it at zero. Passing the game's values to Metal fixed it. F12 · The render thread was copying the level's geometry every frame. In multiplayer and Zombies it copied 23–63 MB of vertex data to the GPU per frame, most of it static. Keeping static buffers resident in Metal brought the copies to 3.5–5 MB per frame: multiplayer 51.8 → 60 fps, Zombies 43.1 → 58.2. The same change does nothing in the campaign, where the pace is set by the scheduler thread. A speed-up helps only the mode whose bottleneck it touches. F13 · A false start inside one instruction cost half the frame rate in combat. In the first conversions from a fresh Steam copy, Zombies fell to 25 fps whenever the player fired. Hot functions were running in the interpreter: the catalogue placed the start of the next function inside the first instruction of a root, so its bounded sweep decoded zero bytes and the root was dropped without a word. Sweeping such roots without the bound, as the one-by-one lifter already did, put them back in the translated code. Predict, then measure. Deterministic record and replay. With every guest thread a coroutine on one host thread, most sources of non-determinism are gone; the replay is checked against the recording, not assumed. Three boundaries capture all outside input: the import dispatcher, the window message drain, and the consumed audio buffers. The journal is about 16 MB. It allows the same run twice with exactly one flag changed. The instrument is the thing that fails. Nearly 200 findings were taken back along the way. The largest share (31%) were an instrument that answered a different question; the next (17%), one that could not answer at all. So every oracle here names its input and refuses to answer when that input is missing. Clean room for the match rules. Multiplayer and Zombies take their match rules from a daily patch file that Steam no longer ships. The replacement in runtime/match_rules/ was written by a team that never saw the original script: one team wrote a behavioural specification from the game, the other wrote the code from that specification alone, and the two only spoke through written questions and answers, kept with their dates. Who does what. AI agents supply the throughput: writing the shims, bisecting millions of calls per run, reading tens of thousands of lines. The human supplies the goal, the corrections from what is really on screen, and refuses the flattering conclusion. This is one game, months of work and heavy manual intervention. You need an Apple silicon Mac, macOS 14 or later, at least 20 GB free (the conversion peaks at about 10 GB and about 4 GB stays), Homebrew, and Steam for Mac signed in to the account that owns the game. git clone https://github.com/adrbn/bo2-mac.git && cd bo2-mac brew install llvm@17 cmake ninja libvpx unicorn pip3 install capstone scripts/make_app.sh --from-source Open Black Ops II.app , point it at your game folder and let it convert: about 1 hour 45 on an M1, the campaign first in about 45 minutes. The campaign is playable as soon as it is converted: play it then, and Zombies and multiplayer are converted when you first pick them in the game's menu. Otherwise the conversion goes on through all three. If the disk falls under 8 GB free, the conversion stops cleanly and resumes where it was. Updating, or if the conversion stops. Run git pull && scripts/make_app.sh --from-source in the repository folder: what is already converted is kept and the conversion resumes. An update redoes only what its changes touch: a fix to the runtime relinks the three modes in about 3 minutes on an M1 instead of converting again. If it still fails, open an issue with the log it names. The converter only accepts the exact Steam build, checked by SHA-256. The Steam executables are encrypted by Valve's SteamStub wrapper and this repository provides no way to remove it : the converter expects the three decrypted images in ~/.bo2-native/steam/ ( t6sp.exe.unpacked.exe , t6mp.exe.unpacked.exe , t6zm.exe.unpacked.exe ). You make them yourself from the copy you bought, with a separate tool of your choice. Only the wrapper must go: the file names above and the SHA-256 check tell you at once whether a file is right. Never share these files. DLC. The launcher asks your Steam client which DLC your account owns, exactly as the game does on Windows. A DLC map plays when you own it and its files are in your game folder. For a copy the user owns, on hardware the user owns. This is an unofficial fan project.
